source.title: Scaling and renormalization in high-dimensional regression
source.authors: Alexander Atanasov; Jacob A. Zavatone-Veth; Cengiz Pehlevan

record.file_problem: No apparent problem; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper derives scaling results in regression models and argues that their exponents and regimes depend on data and model structure. This refines the general scaling-law claim, but it does not empirically test language-model pretraining.
record.gate_note: The paper reviews language-model scaling laws, but its own results concern theoretical and simulated generalization error in linear, kernel, and random-feature regression. Those results bear on the claim's broader extension and setup-dependence versions (V5, V7), not on language-model cross-entropy, extrapolation of large language-model runs, compute-optimal allocation, architecture-shape effects, or downstream-task performance. Cited results from other studies are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: All of the paper's own results are analytic asymptotics, checked by simulation, for ridge, kernel and random-feature regression on synthetic power-law Gaussian data. These are not trained language models (V1–V4, V6), not other modalities or training regimes of neural networks (V5), and not fitting choices behind published laws (V7). Language-model and deep-network scaling appears only as cited background and motivation. The findings show where nontrivial scaling exponents come from in toy linear models, a related but different construct, so they go under fits_no_version rather than as a test of any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors derive generalization error and fine-grained bias-variance decompositions for linear, kernel and random-feature regression via S-transform subordination, and enumerate their scaling regimes. These include a novel variance-dominated regime and nontrivial finite-width exponents from anisotropic weights. They conclude that nontrivial exponents in linear models are not universal but depend on data and target structure, which they call broadly consistent with deep-network observations. They note the free-probability tools likely break down in feature-learning regimes.
record.recipe_differences: The study derives asymptotic formulas using random-matrix and free-probability methods for ridge-regression models; it does not run language-model training sweeps or fit language-model scaling laws.
record.method_sensitivity: The scaling regimes change with covariance and target exponents, ridge strength, label or feature noise, bottleneck choice, and feature-weight structure.

fits_no_version.finding: In ridge, kernel and linear/nonlinear random-feature regression on power-law data, generalization error follows power laws in P and N. The exponents are set by the capacity, source and weight-spectrum exponents, ridge and noise. There are many distinct regimes, including a new variance-over-initialization-dominated regime, and curves can pass through several regimes before reaching the asymptotic rate.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In solvable linear models, scaling exponents are non-universal and determined by data, target and feature-weight spectral structure, with multiple crossover regimes.

record.peer_reviewed: Journal of Statistical Mechanics: Theory and Experiment (2024)
record.problems: The findings are primarily theoretical asymptotics for specified regression models and rely on model assumptions such as Gaussian equivalence and free-probability structure. They do not empirically establish language-model loss scaling or compute-optimal allocation.
record.rows_left_out: Other derived scaling cases and detailed variance decompositions appear across Sections III.I, IV.I, and V.G. The retained rows cover the main power-law regimes and the stated dependence on task/model structure; additional formula variants and illustrative plot values are not separately listed.

untested.parts: No language-model pretraining loss is measured.
No extrapolation from small to large trained runs.
No architecture-shape comparison at fixed parameter count.
No image, video, repeated-data, fine-tuning or transfer experiments with neural networks; only theory for linear and kernel regression.
No fitting of empirical laws and no comparison of parameter counting, schedules or fitting methods. Non-universality of exponents in deep networks is only argued from cited work.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's T5/'tests' classification and its V5/V7 'supports' labels are removed. Toy regression models on synthetic data are not the systems V5 names (neural models in other modalities or regimes). V7 concerns setup and fitting choices in empirical published laws, which the paper only cites. The code URL in the record is likely 'S_transform', with the underscore lost in extraction.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out language-model pretraining cross-entropy scaling with parameters, tokens, or compute.
Whether fits on small language-model runs predict much larger runs.
No fixed-compute optimization of parameter and token counts or their growth rates.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or architecture at fixed parameter count.
The paper derives analogous scaling results for regression models, but does not test image/video models or empirical language-model training regimes.
The paper does not test language-model fitting procedures, parameter-count conventions, training schedules, compute-optimal splits, or published language-law disagreements.

rows.subject: Kernel ridge regression
rows.size_stated: Feature dimension N and sample count P; both taken large in the analysis.
rows.operation_detail: Derives generalization-error scaling for a power-law covariance spectrum and target coefficients.
rows.note: An analytic scaling result for regression generalization error, not language-model cross-entropy.
rows.check: Analytic kernel ridge regression rate on synthetic source/capacity data (Eq. 29). This is not a neural-network or language-model loss, so it cannot show any version's effect. The formula itself is transcribed correctly.

rows.subject: Kernel ridge regression
rows.size_stated: Feature dimension N and sample count P; both taken large in the analysis.
rows.operation_detail: Derives generalization-error scaling in the ridge-dominated regime.
rows.note: The scaling depends on the target source exponent r and differs from the sample-limited regime.
rows.check: Ridge-dominated regime of the same toy model (Eq. 29). It is not the kind of system any version names.

rows.subject: Linear random feature models
rows.size_stated: Input dimension D, feature width N, and sample count P.
rows.operation_detail: Derives target-averaged generalization-error scaling in the bottlenecked regime.
rows.note: The text gives this scaling for the bottlenecked setting; the denominator reflects the stated width/sample-ratio condition.
rows.check: Target-averaged linear random-feature rate in the bottlenecked regime (Sec. IV.I.1). This is a toy model and reproduces Maloney et al. Not a test of any version.

rows.subject: Linear random feature models
rows.size_stated: Input dimension D, feature width N, and sample count P.
rows.operation_detail: Derives target-averaged generalization-error scaling in the overparameterized regime.
rows.note: The formula includes layer-dependent variance factors; for white features the paper gives γ⁽ℓ⁾ = P/Nℓ.
rows.check: Overparameterized linear random-feature rate (Sec. IV.I.1). This is a toy model, not a version's system.

rows.subject: Linear random feature models
rows.size_stated: Input dimension D, feature width N, and sample count P.
rows.operation_detail: Derives general-target signal and variance scaling in the bottlenecked regime.
rows.measure: Generalization error Eg, with separate signal and variance contributions
rows.value: Signal scales as N⁻²ᵅ min(r,1/2); the displayed variance contribution scales as N⁻²ᵅ min(r,1) times the stated γ-dependent factors.
rows.locator: Section IV.I.2, Equation (51) and following scaling expression
rows.note: Distinct exponents for signal and variance components depend on the source exponent and the bottleneck.
rows.check: General-target random-feature exponents (Eq. 51). This is a theoretical toy-model result.

rows.subject: Linear random feature models
rows.size_stated: Feature widths Nℓ and sample count P.
rows.operation_detail: Compares the leading bias/data-variance contribution with feature-initialization variance in the overparameterized ridgeless setting.
rows.value: Bias² + VarX ∼ P⁻²ᵅ min(r,1); VarF + VarXF ∼ P⁻²ᵅ min(r,1/2) Σℓ γ⁽ℓ⁾/(1 − γ⁽ℓ⁾).
rows.locator: Section IV.I.3, Equation (50) and following text
rows.note: The authors define scaling as variance-dominated when the variance term accounts for over half of generalization error.
rows.check: Variance-dominated regime (Sec. IV.I.3, Eq. 50). This is a toy-model bias-variance decomposition, and the 'baseline' field just names a decomposition term.

rows.subject: Linear random feature models with anisotropic weight structure
rows.size_stated: Layer width Nℓ and sample count P.
rows.operation_detail: Analyzes width dependence of variance from structured feature weights.
rows.measure: Variance factor γ⁽ℓ⁾ and resulting finite-width scaling
rows.value: γ⁽ℓ⁾ scales as (P/Nℓ)ᶜ, with c = (1 − αℓ)/αℓ; the paper describes this as nontrivial variance-limited scaling.
rows.note: The authors state that for αℓ > 1 the variance remains finite even as hidden-layer sizes go to infinity.
rows.check: Effect of weight-spectrum structure on finite-width variance. The text writes γ as scaling with (P/Nℓ) in one place and (Nℓ/P)^c in another; the row follows one convention. This is a toy-model result.

rows.subject: Random feature models with additive feature noise
rows.size_stated: Feature width N, input dimension D, and sample count P.
rows.operation_detail: Derives scaling of the effective resolution κ₂ in the ridgeless limit.

conditions.value: σξ²; the text also considers σ̃ξ² = σξ²D

rows.value: When feature noise is negligible, κ₂ ∼ min(P,N)⁻ᵅ; when the additive-noise term dominates, κ₂ ∼ min(P,N)⁻¹σ̃ξ².
rows.locator: Section V.G, Equation (58) and following text
rows.note: This is an effective-resolution scaling, with distinct regimes set by feature-noise strength.
rows.check: Additive-feature-noise model: scaling of the effective ridge κ₂ (Eq. 58). This is an intermediate quantity, not even the error, and it comes from a toy model.
